title: Exposing a Deployment with a Service
intro: Pods get new IPs every time they restart, so nothing can reliably talk to them directly. A Service gives you a stable address. Let's expose the 'web' deployment.

steps.prompt: Expose the 'web' deployment on port 80, targeting container port 80, as a ClusterIP service.
steps.explanation: ClusterIP is the default type — only reachable from inside the cluster. Good for internal service-to-service traffic.
steps.why: 'kubectl expose' is a shortcut that infers the selector from the deployment's own labels. The equivalent full way is writing a Service YAML and 'kubectl apply -f' — you'd do that for anything checked into version control, but expose is faster for one-off setups like this.

steps.fake_output:
NAME   TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)   AGE
web    ClusterIP   10.96.45.210   80/TCP    5s
steps.explanation: That CLUSTER-IP is stable — it won't change even as pods behind it come and go.
steps.why: 'svc' and 'services' are interchangeable, same as 'deploy' vs 'deployments' — kubectl's short aliases exist purely to save typing.

steps.prompt: See which actual pod IPs the service is routing to.
steps.explanation: This is the actual list of pod IPs behind the service — it updates automatically as pods change.
steps.why: You could also check 'kubectl describe svc web' for the same endpoint info bundled with everything else — 'get endpoints' is faster when that's specifically the thing you want to see.

steps.prompt: Get full details on the service.
steps.fake_output:
Name: web
Type: ClusterIP
IP: 10.96.45.210
Port: 80/TCP
Endpoints: 10.244.0.5:80,10.244.0.6:80,10.244.0.7:80
Selector: app=web
steps.explanation: The Selector line is key — the Service finds pods by matching labels, not by name.
steps.why: 'kubectl get svc web -o yaml' shows the raw spec, but describe bundles in the Endpoints and Events sections too — better for confirming the service is actually routing traffic, not just that the object exists.
